implementation_notes: On .NET, the profiling story is excellent (dotnet-trace, dotnet-counters, PerfView, Visual Studio's profiler) but the micro-optimisations that pay are usually runtime-level ones the C# programmer does not control: the GC mode (workstation vs server, concurrent), tiered compilation thresholds, and ReadyToRun versus JIT. The C#-specific wins at a measured hotspot are avoiding boxing (foreach over a List<T> of structs beats IEnumerable<T>, which boxes), avoiding LINQ in a hot loop (each stage allocates an enumerator), struct over class for small value types on the stack, and making a call site monomorphic. The managed-runtime trap is measuring the wrong tier: a method runs unoptimised for the first 30 calls and tiered compilation promotes it later, so a benchmark that does not warm up measures the slow tier.
idiom_name: dotnet-trace/PerfView attribution plus BenchmarkDotNet, applied at the measured hotspot; boxing and allocation are the usual wins
pitfalls: Benchmarking before tiered compilation promotes the method: the first ~30 calls run unoptimised, so a cold benchmark measures the wrong tier.
LINQ in a hot loop allocates an enumerator per stage; the allocation usually dominates the computation and it is invisible without an allocation profiler.
Foreach over IEnumerable<T> of a value type boxes every element; foreach over List<T> does not.
A megamorphic call site is never inlined; making the site monomorphic (a concrete type or a type check) is usually the whole optimisation.
GC mode dominates some workloads: switching workstation/server GC or the GC latency mode can dwarf any source-level micro-optimisation, and it is a config change, not code.
